title: Mansaf
subtitle: Jordanian lamb in fermented yoghurt with rice and flatbread
excerpt: Mansaf is the national dish of Jordan: slow-cooked lamb served on a bed of rice and flatbread and covered in jameed, a pungent fermented dried yoghurt sauce. It is a feast dish, served at weddings and celebrations on a large communal platter, eaten standing around the table with the right hand.
sourceNotes: Jordan's national dish. Traditionally made with jameed, a hard fermented dried yoghurt from the Bedouin tradition. Outside Jordan, strained yoghurt or labneh thinned with water is the standard substitute.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The lamb can be slow-cooked a day ahead and reheated in the sauce. Assemble the platter just before serving.

content.text: Mansaf is a dish of scale and ceremony. In Jordan it is cooked in large pots and served on enormous platters at weddings and community gatherings, eaten communally without cutlery. It is intensely savoury: the lamb braised in yoghurt sauce has a distinctive tang and richness that is unlike any other lamb dish.

The sauce is the defining element. Traditionally made with jameed (hard, salted, fermented dried goat's milk), it has a sharp, almost funky depth. Outside Jordan, thick strained yoghurt or labneh thinned with a little water and warmed carefully gives a similar result.
The key technical rule: never boil the yoghurt sauce at a high heat. It must simmer gently or it will split and become grainy.

items.prepNote: full-fat, or labneh thinned with 200 ml water
torn into pieces as the base

content.text: Place the lamb in a large pot with the onion, bay leaves, allspice, turmeric, and salt. Cover with 2 litres of water. Bring to the boil, skim off any foam, then reduce to a low simmer. Cook covered for 1.5 to 2 hours until the lamb is very tender and falling from the bone. Remove the lamb and reserve the stock.

Measure 700 ml of the reserved lamb stock into a saucepan. Add the rinsed rice and bring to the boil. Reduce to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 15 minutes until the stock is absorbed and the rice is tender.

Beat the egg into the yoghurt. Pour into a saucepan and heat gently over low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon in one direction to prevent splitting. Once the yoghurt is hot and steaming, add 400 ml of the remaining lamb stock. Stir to combine and keep on a very gentle simmer for 10 minutes. Do not boil.

Lay the torn flatbread pieces across a large platter. Mound the rice on top. Place the lamb pieces over the rice. Pour half the yoghurt sauce over everything. Scatter with toasted pine nuts and parsley. Serve the remaining sauce in a bowl alongside.

rows.symptom: Yoghurt sauce splits and turns grainy
rows.cause: Heat too high or heated without stirring
rows.fix: Add the beaten egg before heating; it stabilises the protein. Stir constantly in one direction over low heat only.
Continue braising for another 30 minutes. Mansaf lamb should fall apart at a nudge.

rows.cause: Too much stock or cooked at too high a heat
rows.fix: Use exactly 700 ml stock for 500 g rice. Keep the heat very low once covered.

content.text: If you can find jameed (sold in Jordanian or Palestinian grocery shops in the UK), dissolve the hard block in warm water and use instead of the yoghurt for a more authentic sauce. Serve with a simple chopped tomato and cucumber salad on the side.
Braise the lamb and prepare the stock a day ahead. Refrigerate separately. Cook the rice and make the yoghurt sauce fresh when serving; the sauce does not keep well once made.

Mansaf is the national dish of Jordan. It is eaten at weddings, at funerals, at Eid celebrations, and whenever a community gathers around food. The Bedouin tradition of eating standing around a communal platter is where the dish comes from. It has spread through the Levant and is also eaten in parts of Palestine, Syria, and Saudi Arabia.
